The transition from perceived duration to the when of memory is likely shaped by attention and working memory (WM). In two experiments, we investigated how memory decay, interference between stored durations, and internal versus external attention affect the precision of recall from temporal WM. For this, we used a delayed reproduction task in which participants listened to a sequence of time intervals and reproduced them after a retention period (Herbst et al., 2025). In Experiment 1, we manipulated the ratio between the target interval and the retention interval, showing that both the duration of the retention interval (decay) and its ratio to the target (temporal distinctiveness yielding interference) affected WM performance. In Experiment 2, we examined interference between intervals within a sequence by manipulating attention via a cue indicating which interval to reproduce. The cue appeared either before (pro-cue) or after (retro-cue) the retention period, directing external attention to sensory encoding or internal attention to WM representations, respectively, either for a single item or the full sequence. External attention selectively benefited accuracy and precision for the longest item when cued alone in the final position. Retro-cueing, by contrast, more generally reduced precision for single-item compared to the whole-sequence recall. Finally, a mixture modeling approach revealed swap errors consistent with those observed in visual WM. Together, these findings compare the contributions of decay and temporal distinctiveness to temporal WM performance with a dynamic resource allocation
